visuals.pageTitle: Understand multi-omics, one question at a time
visuals.heading: The map
visuals.label: Foundations: molecules and cells · DNA: change and copy state · RNA: message and form · Protein: product and state · Function: controlled response · Clinical evidence and benefit
visuals.caption: The arrows name questions to investigate. A measured box does not guarantee the next one. Check cell identity, location and sample time at every layer. Blood time series add repeated assay-specific snapshots; eligibility and benefit still need their own clinical evidence. Use the lesson table for each linked step.

explanation: A blood-based ctDNA or MRD result tells you what a particular assay detected in that blood sample, on that date. Repeated samples can show whether the measured signal is rising, falling, or staying undetectable. That may provide information about molecular disease burden or change over time—especially when interpreted with the assay’s units, denominator, detection limit, and sampling schedule Read blood measurements as a time series. It cannot, by itself, tell you: where any cancer is located; whether detected DNA comes from living, treatment-sensitive tumor cells; whether undetectable means “no cancer anywhere”; whether a scan finding is cancer or treatment-related change; which treatment will help, or whether changing treatment will improve survival.

In this cartoon, the key warning is that each measured layer—or blood snapshot—answers only its own question; detection is not the same as location, biological activity, or clinical benefit. A useful way to think about it is a smoke alarm: a signal may warn that something needs checking, but it does not show where the fire is or prove that putting out one room’s smoke will solve the problem. Would you like to focus next on a rising result, an undetectable result, or disagreement between ctDNA and imaging?
